Pollachius pollachius.fieldNote: A benthopelagic hunter that hangs above kelp forests and wrecks. Look for a dark lateral line strongly arched over the pectoral fin, a projecting lower jaw and no chin barbel.

Pollachius virens.fieldNote: A member of the pollack family with a dusky greenish-brown back and sides, a silvery white belly, and a straight, smooth, pale lateral line running the whole length of the flank. The upper and lower jaws are about equal in length, where the pollack has a projecting lower jaw and a dark lateral line that curves sharply over the pectoral fin. An active, gregarious fish of inshore and offshore water, also called coalfish or coley.

Trisopterus luscus.fieldNote: A deep-bodied, coppery member of the cod family with three or four pale vertical bands, a long chin barbel, and a black mark the size of the eye at the base of each pectoral fin. Gregarious, in large schools when young, and often found in and around wrecks.

Merlangius merlangus.fieldNote: A slim, cod-like fish, blue-green above and silvery-white below, with three close-set dorsal fins and two anal fins. The chin barbel is rudimentary or absent, a small dark spot marks the base of each pectoral fin, and the brown (not black) lateral line separates it from a haddock.

Labrus bergylta.fieldNote: Stocky wrasse with thick lips and a long spiny dorsal fin; colours vary from green to red-brown with pale spots.

Labrus mixtus.fieldNote: Two looks. Older males have a dark blue head with brilliant blue lines and blotches along the flanks, over a bright orange body and fins. Females are rose-pink to orange-red with 2 to 3 dark spots, interspersed with white, on the rear dorsal fin and the adjacent tail fin. Young males look like females but lack those spots.

Symphodus melops.fieldNote: A deep-bodied wrasse of rocky shores and seaweed, with a black spot in the middle of the tail stalk and a comma-shaped spot behind the eye.

Ctenolabrus rupestris.fieldNote: The smallest wrasse in British and Irish waters: slender, brown, greenish or orange-red, and told from every other wrasse by two dark patches, one at the front of the dorsal fin and one just in front of the tail fin.

Conger conger.fieldNote: A long, powerful grey-brown eel with scaleless skin and the dorsal, tail and anal fins fused into one continuous fringe. It spends the day in a hole or crevice in rock or a wreck and becomes active at night to hunt.

Pholis gunnellus.fieldNote: Slippery ribbon-like fish with a row of dark-and-pale ocelli along the dorsal fin.

Gobiusculus flavescens.fieldNote: A small, slender goby up to 6 cm, reddish to greenish brown, with a black spot at the base of the tail fin; males carry a second, smaller spot beneath the pectoral fin. Unlike other gobies it hovers in small, loose shoals in the water column among kelp and eelgrass rather than sitting on the bottom.

Pomatoschistus microps.fieldNote: Once confused with the sand goby, but the common goby carries a dark mark at the top of the base of the pectoral fin. It tolerates a wide range of salinity and prefers low-salinity water, so it is abundant in estuaries, saltmarshes and intertidal pools all round the British and Irish coasts, usually in under a metre of water.

Gobius paganellus.fieldNote: A moderately large goby of rocky shores and pools, growing to about 12 cm, dark brown or pale brown with dark mottling, with a rounded head and large close-set eyes. The tell is the pale band along the upper margin of the first dorsal fin: creamy or yellowy in females, bright yellow to orange in males.

Pomatoschistus minutus.fieldNote: A small pale brown or grey goby of sandy and muddy bottoms, marked darker along the sides; it takes its colour from the seabed and buries itself in the sediment when a predator comes.

Callionymus lyra.fieldNote: Flat, scaleless bottom fish that lies part-buried in sand or shell gravel; the first dorsal fin is tall and sail-like, and mature males have elongate dorsal and caudal fin rays.

Callionymus maculatus.fieldNote: A small dragonet of sandy bottoms, and a deeper-water fish than its common relative, recorded between 45 and 650 m where the common dragonet is given as 1 to 440 m and usually 5 to 30 m. It reaches 17 cm, well short of the common dragonet's 30.5 cm. The gill cover carries four spines, and the male's dorsal fin has four spots in a row where the female has two.

Pleuronectes platessa.fieldNote: Right-eyed flatfish with bright orange spots scattered across a brown back.

Limanda limanda.fieldNote: A right-eyed flatfish of sandy ground, brown with darker blotches and small speckles. The skin on its upper side feels rough where plaice and flounder feel smooth, and the lateral line is strongly arched into a semi-circular curve over the pectoral fin. Some dab carry a few orange spots, but not as well developed as a plaice's.

Platichthys flesus.fieldNote: A dull brown to greenish-grey flatfish of estuaries and tidal rivers, and the only European flatfish that penetrates far up an estuary and lives in fresh water for long periods. Finely toothed tubercles run between the rays of the dorsal and anal fins and along the lateral line, so it feels rough where related flatfish are smooth. Many fish carry irregular reddish or orange spots on the upper side, but not as bright as a plaice's.

Scyliorhinus canicula.fieldNote: A slender greyish-brown shark speckled with numerous small dark spots, both dorsal fins set far back towards the tail. Nocturnal: by day it rests on the seabed or hides in caves and crevices.

Mullus surmuletus.fieldNote: Red and brown stripes run the length of a moderately elongate body, and a pair of long chin barbels hangs under the jaw. Snuffles through the sediment for buried crustaceans, worms and molluscs.

Trisopterus minutus.fieldNote: A slender, coppery member of the cod family with a barbel under the chin and a dark blotch at the base of the pectoral fin, commonly about 20 cm long. Gregarious, living in small schools over sand and mud, and small fish are often seen around wrecks and in cracks and crevices in rock.

Gadus morhua.fieldNote: Heavy-bodied cod with three dorsal and two anal fins, a chin barbel, and a curved pale lateral line.

Chelon labrosus.fieldNote: A silvery, elongate mullet with a thick upper lip, it keeps to the bottom in shallow inshore water and gathers in schools, often running up into brackish lagoons and fresh water.

Dicentrarchus labrax.fieldNote: A thick-set, silvery fish with a black or blue back and two entirely separate dorsal fins, the first spiny. Young bass school together; adults keep to smaller numbers and hunt small pelagic fish.

Trachurus trachurus.fieldNote: A slender, silvery schooling fish with tall keeled scales along the side and a black spot on the trailing edge of the gill cover.

Scomber scombrus.fieldNote: A fast, streamlined shoaling fish. Strong dark markings cross the back, oblique to near-vertical with relatively little undulation, above an unmarked belly of silver and metallic blue.

Sprattus sprattus.fieldNote: A shiny silver to grey schooling fish of inshore waters, with a very forked tail and a strong keel of scutes along the belly.

Atherina presbyter.fieldNote: Slender silvery fish with a brilliant stripe from head to tail and a translucent greenish back; schools near the surface in coastal water and estuaries.

Taurulus bubalis.fieldNote: A scaleless rocky-shore ambush predator with very large eyes and mouth, a spiny head carrying one very long cheek spine, and colouring that matches its surroundings with great accuracy.

Lipophrys pholis.fieldNote: A smooth, scaleless blenny of rocky shores, up to about 16 to 17 cm, with no tentacles on the head and a single long dorsal fin split by a notch into unequal sections. Its colour varies with the surroundings, from dark brown or blotched to blackish, with a dark spot behind the first dorsal fin. It shelters in rockpools and under damp stones and seaweed, emerges at high tide to forage, and can breathe air while out of water.

Spinachia spinachia.fieldNote: A very slender fish with 14-17 isolated spines along the back in front of the dorsal fin, a tapering snout with a tiny mouth, and a long narrow tail stalk ending in a small rounded tail fin. Brown or olive above and paler below, sometimes with dark bars on the flanks. It lives singly or in pairs among weed on shorelines and in inshore water less than 20 m deep.

Carcinus maenas.fieldNote: A very common crab found on all shores of Britain and Ireland, from high water down to 60 m. The shell is much broader than long, with five sharp teeth either side of the eyes and three rounded lobes between them. Colour is highly variable, most often mottled olive green to dark brown, but sometimes orange or red. The walking legs end in points, and the last segment of the rear legs is flattened but never expanded into a swimming paddle.

Cancer pagurus.fieldNote: Unmistakable once you've seen one: a broad reddish-brown shell with a crimped 'pie-crust' edge and big black-tipped pincers. Small ones hide under stones on the lower shore, while the dinner-plate-sized adults live in deeper water.

Necora puber.fieldNote: Feisty and quick to raise its claws. The shell is covered in fine velvety fur, the back legs end in flattened swimming paddles, and the eyes are a startling red. Brownish, on sheltered rocky shores.

Liocarcinus depurator.fieldNote: A swimming crab of fine muddy sand and gravel, found on all British and Irish coasts from the lower shore down to over 300 m. The shell is broader than long, about 51 mm wide, with five pointed teeth along each front side edge and rows of hairs across it. The body is pale reddish-brown, and the give-away is the violet-tinted paddle on the last pair of legs. Although it is a swimming crab it normally crawls on the seabed, and only really swims in extremis.

Majoidea.fieldNote: A long-legged crab whose shell narrows at the front to a short forked rostrum projecting between the eyes. Legs 2 to 5 are long, slender and spider-like, the first pair carries the pincers, and the shell is usually covered with algae or encrusting invertebrates. The great spider crab has a pear-shaped shell and is found around all British coasts, though it is less common in the south and west. The larger common spider crab has a circular to oval shell, broad at the back and narrow at the front, reaches 20 cm in body length, and lives in south and west Britain and Ireland.

Pagurus bernhardus.fieldNote: A hermit crab. Its soft, coiled abdomen is tucked inside an empty sea snail shell, any suitable one from a periwinkle to a common whelk. Only the legs and knobbly claws show, the right one much larger than the left, and the whole animal can pull back inside the shell if it senses a threat. A sea anemone or a hydroid sometimes rides on the shell.

Sepia officinalis.fieldNote: A broad, flattened cephalopod, oval in cross-section, with a paired fin running from behind the head to the tip of the body, eight arms and two long tentacles it shoots out to seize prey. The largest cuttlefish in UK waters, it buries in sand by day and changes colour very rapidly.

Loligo forbesii.fieldNote: A long, slender, cylindrical squid whose paired fins form an elongate diamond running about three quarters of the mantle. Pink, red and brown predominate, with flame-like purplish stripes along the mantle. It gathers near the bottom by day and rises into the water column at night.

Loligo vulgaris.fieldNote: Very like the veined squid but with shorter rear fins (a little over half the body length). A fast, torpedo-bodied schooler of open shelf water, reddish and quick to flush pale.

Sepiola atlantica.fieldNote: A thumbnail-sized cephalopod (also called the Little Cuttlefish) with a stubby rounded body and small ear-like fins. Buries in clean sand by day with just its eyes showing, and is flecked with iridescent specks.

Eledone cirrhosa.fieldNote: Our commonest octopus: a smooth, sac-like body and eight long arms that curl at the tips, each arm with a SINGLE row of suckers (the key difference from the common octopus). Orange-brown, tucked into rocky crevices.

Octopus vulgaris.fieldNote: Bulbous-headed with eight arms and warty skin, changing colour and texture in a blink. Each arm carries TWO rows of suckers (vs the single row of the curled octopus). Dens in rock holes; mostly a southern and western visitor.

Asterina gibbosa.fieldNote: A small, fat-armed star shaped almost like a five-pointed cushion. Slightly puffy and fleshy, greenish-grey to orange, found tucked under stones on the lower shore.

Marthasterias glacialis.fieldNote: Big and unmistakable: five long tapering arms lined with three rows of white spines, each spine ringed with blue at its base. Pale grey-green, on rocky shores; large ones can span a forearm.

Asterias rubens.fieldNote: The classic orange five-armed star. The arms taper to a point and carry a knobbly central line of pale spines but no big spikes. Turns up almost anywhere, often near mussel beds.

Ophiothrix fragilis.fieldNote: A small spiny disc trailing five long, thread-thin arms that writhe and snap off at a touch. Colour is hugely variable; often carpets the seabed in dense beds and hides under stones.

Patella vulgata.fieldNote: A plain ridged cone clamped tight to bare rock, with no spire and no pattern. Each one grazes its own patch of algae and homes back to the same scar as the tide drops.

Nucella lapillus.fieldNote: A thick, short-spired shell with spiral ridges and an oval mouth drawn out into a little spout. White, grey or banded brown (the colour follows its diet). Drills neat holes through barnacles and mussels.

Calliostoma zizyphinum.fieldNote: A glossy, sharply conical shell with straight sides and a flat base, like a smooth spinning top. Marbled pink and white over 10 to 12 finely ribbed whorls, with no open navel beneath.

Steromphala umbilicalis.fieldNote: A squat, bluntly conical top shell, greenish with widely spaced reddish-purple bands. Flatter than the pointed top shells, with a tell-tale open 'navel' hole at the centre of the underside.

Aurelia aurita.fieldNote: Our commonest jellyfish and harmless to touch. A flat, translucent bluish bell with four pale horseshoe rings (the gonads) showing through the top, and only a short fringe of fine tentacles beneath.

Chrysaora hysoscella.fieldNote: A flattish pale bell marked with dark brown V-shapes radiating from the centre like the points of a compass. Trails long thin tentacles and four frilly arms. It stings, so look but don't touch.

Cyanea capillata.fieldNote: Our biggest jellyfish: a broad reddish-brown bell trailing a dense mane of dozens of long, fine tentacles. Delivers a painful sting and is most common in northern waters in summer.

Rhizostoma octopus.fieldNote: A huge, solid, dome-shaped bell (the 'dustbin-lid' jelly) with NO long trailing tentacles. Underneath hang eight thick, frilly cauliflower-like arms. Mostly harmless despite its size.

Cyanea lamarckii.fieldNote: Like a smaller lion's mane but a translucent purplish-blue, the colour deepening towards the top of the bell. Many slender trailing tentacles beneath; a mild stinger of inshore waters.

Pelagia noctiluca.fieldNote: A small mauve-to-purple bell densely peppered with stinging warts, trailing eight long tentacles and four frilly arms. Glows blue in the dark and arrives in swarms; a notable stinger, increasingly seen in UK waters.

Eutrigla gurnardus.fieldNote: Elongated, armour-headed seabed fish that 'walks' on three free finger-like rays beneath each large fan-shaped pectoral fin. Greyish-brown with a white-spotted, nearly straight side-line; the dark blotch on the first (spiny) dorsal fin is the giveaway.

Chelidonichthys cuculus.fieldNote: Brick-red gurnard with an armoured head and the family's three free finger-like pectoral rays for 'walking' the seabed. A conspicuous row of bony plates runs along the straight side-line; pectoral fins are plain reddish (no bold patch). Smaller than the tub gurnard.

Chelidonichthys lucerna.fieldNote: The largest UK gurnard: reddish, armour-headed, walking on three free finger-like pectoral rays. The give-away is the enormous fan pectoral fins, vivid peacock-blue and green with a bright blue edge, flared when it moves.

Chelidonichthys lastoviza.fieldNote: Gurnard whose reddish body is covered in many fine dark OBLIQUE streaks, the give-away. Armoured head and three free finger-like pectoral rays for 'walking' the seabed like its cousins; deeper-bodied than the grey gurnard.

Echinus esculentus.fieldNote: Britain's largest urchin, a reddish-pink to purple dome up to 16cm across, covered in short even spines with a five-part radial pattern showing through. Grazes algae off rock and kelp stipes with a mouth on its underside; edible, and once commercially harvested.

Psammechinus miliaris.fieldNote: A small green urchin, its short spines tipped with violet-purple, giving a speckled two-tone look. Common in shallow rockpools, kelp holdfasts and seagrass beds all around the UK, often the first urchin a rockpooler finds.

Paracentrotus lividus.fieldNote: A dark purple to blackish urchin of rock pools and shallow reefs in the south and west, often sitting in a shallow pit it has worn into the rock. Longer spines than the green urchin; found on south-western and Irish coasts, absent from the North Sea.

Echinocardium cordatum.fieldNote: Egg-shaped and covered in short, fine, backward-pointing spines like fur, living buried 10-20cm down in clean sand. Almost never seen alive and in the open; what washes up on beaches is the pale, heart-marked test with its five petal-shaped pore patterns.

Spatangus purpureus.fieldNote: A larger, purplish-brown heart urchin covered in dense short spines, ploughing shallow trails just under the surface of clean sand and gravel in deeper subtidal water. Bigger and hairier-looking than the sea potato, with a distinct heart-shaped outline.

Phalacrocorax aristotelis.fieldNote: A slim, all-dark diving bird with a thin hooked bill and, in breeding adults, a small forward-curling crest. Glossy bottle-green to black plumage with a purple sheen; dives from the surface to hunt fish, often staying under for 20-40 seconds. The commonest inshore diving bird on rocky UK coasts, easily confused with the cormorant.

Phalacrocorax carbo.fieldNote: Bigger and bulkier than the shag, with a heavier build, a longer neck, and a patch of yellow-orange bare skin around the base of the bill and chin. Bronzy-black overall; breeding adults show a white throat patch and white thigh flash. Dives to chase fish, then perches upright on rocks or posts with wings held open to dry.

Somateria mollissima.fieldNote: The heaviest UK duck. Males are boldly pied black and white with a pale green nape patch and a long sloping profile running from the forehead straight into the bill; females are warm mottled brown all over, both with the same wedge-shaped head. Dives to feed on mussels and other shellfish, often around shellfish farms, and rafts in large flocks just offshore.

Halichoerus grypus.fieldNote: The larger UK seal, with a long straight 'Roman nose' profile and widely spaced nostrils that sit parallel. Coat is blotchy and irregularly patched, grey to brown with large dark and pale patches. Hauls out on rocky shores and offshore islands around most of the UK coast, especially in autumn to breed.

Phoca vitulina.fieldNote: Smaller and daintier than the grey seal, with a short rounded 'button' muzzle, a concave forehead profile, and V-shaped nostrils that meet at the bottom. Coat is finely speckled with small dark spots rather than blotches. Often hauls out on sandbanks and rocks at low tide in a curved 'banana' pose, and is more likely to be seen in estuaries and harbours than the grey seal.
